title: Beyond the three gunas
hookLine: Arjuna asks what a person beyond the three threads looks like
carry: beyond the three gunas, through devotion
last: TAMAS STRIKES, RAJAS BINDS, SATTVA SHOWS THE ROAD.

cards: Post something online and watch what happens to you. A hundred likes, and you feel tall. One cruel comment, and it rattles around your head all night.

The hundred don't cancel out the one. Plenty of people are built this way: praise lifts, blame drops, and managing both takes a lot of energy. At the end of chapter fourteen, Arjuna asks a very practical question.
What does someone look like who has gone beyond the three threads? How do they act? How do they get there?

teach.h: THE THREADS STILL COME AND GO.
teach.b: Arjuna's question is verse twenty-one, and it has three parts: the marks, the behavior, the way. Krishna answers with a portrait.
Verse twenty-two: when light, activity and confusion come, this person doesn't hate them; when they go, doesn't long for them. The threads still show up.
Even the person beyond the gunas has sleepy mornings and busy afternoons. The difference is the grip.
Verse twenty-three: they sit like someone unconcerned, udasina, literally sitting above, not shaken by the gunas, knowing it's just the threads moving.

teach.h: CLAY, STONE AND GOLD, THE SAME.
teach.b: Verse twenty-four: the same in sorrow and happiness, resting in the self; a lump of clay, a stone and gold are all the same to them.
The same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and in praise of themselves. Verse twenty-five: the same in honor and dishonor, the same to friend and enemy.
That person, Krishna says, has gone beyond the gunas. Gunatita. Then the answer to the third question, how to get there.
Verse twenty-six: the one who serves me with unwavering devotion goes beyond the three and becomes fit for Brahman.

So the way beyond isn't a technique for crushing the threads. In this chapter, it's bhakti, love. Verse twenty-seven closes: I am the ground of Brahman, of the deathless, of lasting dharma, and of perfect joy.
This isn't indifference. It's the steadiness of someone whose center is somewhere the likes and comments can't reach.

how: Hindu teachers hold up the gunatita of Gita 14.22–14.25 as a picture of spiritual maturity; many devotional traditions point to 14.26, unwavering devotion, as the way there.

o: feeling nothing at all, numb to joy and pain
free of every quality, a blank, empty mind
gone beyond the three gunas, gripped by none

games.q: the one beyond the three — tap the pairs.

s: the person beyond the gunas never feels sleepy or busy again
verse 22: the threads still come; they just don't hate or long for them.
the same in blame and praise is one of the marks in verse 24
the same in blame and in praise of themselves.
in chapter 14, the way beyond the three is devotion
verse 26: unwavering devotion takes a person beyond the three.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've heard the three threads bind everyone. what do you ask next?
o: which thread is best to keep?
what marks the one beyond them, how do they act, how do they get there?
can I skip the threads by leaving the battle?
games.why: verse 21: Arjuna asks all three, and Krishna answers with a portrait and one way: unwavering devotion.

practice: Remember a recent word of praise and let it land; notice the lift in the chest. Then a recent word of blame, and notice the drop. If you pray, offer both to God, the way verse twenty-six points.
If you don't, simply sit a little above both, like someone watching weather from a hill: the lift and the drop still come; you're just not living inside them.

wordCard.voice: Gunatita, gone beyond the gunas. Gita fourteen: the one who has gone beyond the gunas doesn't hate them when they come or long for them when they go, and is the same in praise and blame.

orig.note: Sanskrit: gunatita, gone beyond the gunas (guna + atita, gone beyond).

carryVoice: Your line: beyond the three gunas, through devotion. The threads still come; love loosens their grip. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.22–14.25 (marks of the one beyond the gunas)
Bhagavad Gita 14.26–14.27 (devotion; the ground of Brahman)
